title: How to Check Two Tests When Both Can Miss — Hui & Walter (1980) Two-Population Latent-Class Identifiability, Joseph Beta Priors & Bayesian Conditional-Dependence Diagnostic Models Without a Gold Standard

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: How do you measure a diagnostic test's accuracy when the 'gold standard' test can also miss cases? Hui and Walter (1980) proved that running two imperfect tests across two populations with different disease rates unlocks all sensitivities and specificities—provided errors are independent or modeled with Bayesian priors.
teenKit.whyItMatters: In infectious disease and pathology, treating an imperfect reference test as 100% infallible makes a more sensitive new test look falsely 'wrong.'
keyTakeaways: Cross-classifying two binary tests in one population yields only 3 independent degrees of freedom for 5 unknowns (prevalence plus two sensitivities and two specificities).
Adding a second population with distinct prevalence adds 3 more degrees of freedom for just 1 new unknown, reaching 6 equations for 6 parameters under conditional independence.
When two tests share a biological blind spot (conditional dependence), Lawrence Joseph and Dendukuri showed how informative Beta priors restore Bayesian identifiability.

vocab.meaning: A statistical model where true disease status is treated as unobserved ('latent') and inferred from multiple imperfect measurements.
The number of independent cell counts in a contingency table available to estimate unknown parameters.
The assumption that, given a patient's true disease state, Test A's chance of error is unrelated to Test B's chance of error.

quiz.question: In the classic Hui–Walter design with 2 binary tests across 2 populations, how many independent data degrees of freedom match how many unknown parameters?
quiz.explanation: Each 2x2 table contributes 3 independent cell probabilities (3 + 3 = 6), matching 2 prevalences + 2 sensitivities + 2 specificities = 6 parameters.
